rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the elution window and critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A 10-minute gradient provides a useful baseline near the scoring time target.

Change only gradient duration to determine whether the crowded early cluster separates with a shallower slope. This also tests how much resolution can be gained before trimming the gradient window to recover time.

The shallow gradient improves the crowded cluster but incurs a time penalty. Raising temperature at the original slope tests whether selectivity can resolve that cluster while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.

Keep the favorable high-temperature selectivity and make the gradient shallower to improve the remaining critical pair. The last peak should still elute within 10 minutes, leaving room to reach full resolution without a time penalty.

The remaining critical pair worsened with a shallower gradient, so test a steeper gradient at the favorable temperature. This will show whether its resolution can improve before another pair becomes limiting.

The critical pair barely benefits from changing slope, so test temperature-dependent selectivity instead. A 5 °C step below the best run will clarify whether an intermediate temperature can resolve the cluster while retaining a sub-10-minute elution time.

Keep the best temperature and shift the starting organic fraction to alter selectivity in the early cluster. This tests a different gradient window because slope changes alone have not resolved the limiting pair.
Injection 7 reached the maximum CRF; now shorten the gradient by one grid step to seek a faster fully resolved method. Retain injection 7 as the benchmark if either critical pair falls below R = 1.5.

Slightly narrow the gradient window to recover resolution for both marginal pairs while retaining the shorter programmed gradient. The last peak eluted near 0.64 organic in injection 8, so an endpoint of 0.85 leaves ample elution strength.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to test whether the fully resolved method can be accelerated through a window shift. Monitor the early cluster closely, since stronger initial solvent may compress its separation.

The high-temperature window is now tightly constrained by the early cluster. Test the opposite temperature limit for a different elution order that might support a faster fully resolved method, retaining injection 9 as the fastest maximum-score method so far.

Return to the favorable high-temperature selectivity and test the endpoint between injections 8 and 9. This brackets the steepest gradient that might retain full resolution while shortening the fastest maximum-score method.

Trim the high-organic portion of the gradient and reduce its programmed duration while keeping a slightly shallower slope than injection 9. This should preserve full resolution, with the last peak expected near the gradient endpoint.
Increase the endpoint one step to test a slope between the fully resolved injection 9 and marginal injection 12. This may shorten last-peak elution while preserving R ≥ 1.5 for the limiting pair.

Injection 14 still has a sub-threshold pair despite its rounded CRF, so injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method. Test whether a shallower gradient at phi0 = 0.20 restores the compressed pair while providing more balanced resolution margins.

Return to the best starting fraction and reduce the slope to build resolution margin around the fully resolved injection 9. This tests a more robust maximum-score alternative while keeping the last peak comfortably below 10 minutes.

Test the intermediate endpoint between injections 9 and 16 to balance speed against resolution margin. Both neighboring methods fully resolved the mixture, so this should retain maximum CRF with a last-peak time near 6.4 minutes.

Test the remaining starting-fraction grid point near the best window to check whether selectivity changes nonlinearly between phi0 = 0.05 and 0.15. Injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved benchmark.

Test whether slightly lower temperature restores separation of the limiting pair at phi0 = 0.20 without losing the neighboring pair’s resolution margin. This checks a coupled temperature/window adjustment that could provide another fully resolved method.

Retain the successful starting fraction and temperature, and test a shallower gradient for additional resolution margin without a time penalty. Injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method; this run explores a more robust maximum-score alternative.

At phi0 = 0.20, injection 15 nearly resolved the limiting pair; this slightly shallower slope should bring it above R = 1.5. The endpoint remains above the estimated last-peak elution fraction, making this a promising additional maximum-score method.

Trim injection 20’s unused high-organic tail while retaining nearly the same favorable slope. This should preserve its resolution margin with a shorter programmed gradient and last-peak elution around 7.2 minutes; injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Reduce the endpoint one step from injection 22 to test additional resolution margin while keeping the last peak within 10 minutes. The estimated last-peak elution fraction is about 0.59, so 0.65 should still provide sufficient elution strength.

Match injection 16’s fully resolving slope while trimming the programmed gradient to six minutes. The last peak may elute briefly into the final hold, but should remain comfortably below 10 minutes; injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Use the final injection for a maximum-score candidate with a slope bracketed by fully resolved injections 16 and 22, targeting additional resolution margin while remaining below 10 minutes. Injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method at a last-peak time of 6.04 minutes.
